notes.b: Young children depend entirely on adults to meet their basic needs for growth and survival. If a physical need is missed, the child's health and development suffer, so each one matters.
points: Food: a balanced diet in suitable amounts supports growth, and new foods are introduced as the child grows so that the body gets all the nutrients it needs.
Shelter: a warm, dry, safe home protects children from weather and hazards, because young children cannot regulate their body temperature or avoid danger for themselves.
Clothing: suitable clothing protects against cold and injury and allows free movement, so the child can play and explore.
Sleep and rest: regular sleep supports growth, concentration and the repair of the body.
Health care: regular check-ups, immunisation (vaccination against disease) and prompt treatment of illness prevent disease and support healthy development.
Hygiene: washing, care of teeth and toilet training prevent infection, because germs spread easily where hygiene is poor.
Safety and protection: supervision and safe surroundings prevent accidents and abuse, since young children cannot recognise danger.
notes.tip: When asked for the needs of a young child, name the need and then say its effect on the child, for example immunisation prevents disease. Keep physical needs in a separate list from psychological needs.

notes.b: Children need more than food and shelter. Their emotional and mental needs shape how confident they feel and how well they relate to others, now and as adults.
points: Love and affection: warm physical and verbal affection helps children feel valued, so they grow up believing they matter.
Security and trust: a dependable, consistent caregiver teaches children that the world is predictable and safe.
Attachment: a strong bond with a consistent caregiver forms the basis for later relationships, because the child learns what a trusting relationship feels like.
Praise and encouragement: recognising effort builds self-esteem (belief in your own worth) and motivation.
Stimulation and learning: play, conversation, reading and exploration develop language and thinking.
Routine and boundaries: consistent limits help children learn self-control and understand expectations.
Social contact: interaction within the family teaches children to form friendships and relate to others.
notes.tip: Name the need, then explain its effect on the child, for example praise builds self-esteem. Examiners look for this explanation, so a bare list loses marks.

notes.b: How well a child's needs are met in the early years affects the adult they become.
points: When physical and psychological needs are met, children grow into well-adjusted, confident adults who are able to contribute to society.
When needs go unmet, children are more likely to grow up insecure, with poor self-esteem and difficulty forming relationships.
notes.tip: End an answer on needs by tying them to well-adjusted adults who contribute to society, as exam answers do.

notes.b: Adolescents are changing quickly in body and mind. They still need care, but they need it in a different form from young children, with more freedom and respect.
points: Growth: rapid growth (the growth spurt) increases the body's need for energy, protein, calcium and iron, and adequate physical activity supports healthy development.
Sleep: adolescents need extended sleep because they are growing, and changes in their body clock can make early starts difficult.
Independence: adolescents need increasing freedom to make choices, with parents gradually reducing direct control while keeping limits.
Identity and self-esteem: adolescents build a personal identity through relationships, interests and feedback from others.
Peer acceptance: friendships become central, so a safe place at home to meet friends supports them.
Privacy: adolescents need personal space and private time, which parents should respect, because it helps them develop their own identity.
Emotional support: adolescents need to be listened to without judgement when problems arise, so they feel able to turn to parents.
Guidance on risks: adolescents benefit from advice on the risks they meet, so they can make safe choices as they gain independence.
notes.tip: Do not give amounts of nutrients for adolescents. Name the need and explain it, for example independence is needed because they are preparing for adult life.

notes.h: How the family meets children's needs
notes.b: The family is where children's needs are met day to day, mostly through ordinary routines and the way adults behave.
points: Daily routines: regular meal, sleep and homework times give structure and security, so the child knows what to expect.
Modelling: children learn behaviour, language and values by watching how adults act.
Teaching: parents teach self-care, manners, safety and social skills during everyday activities.
Health monitoring: parents arrange medical care, watch for illness and promote healthy eating and exercise.
Responsiveness: a prompt response to a child's distress builds attachment and trust.
The home is where language, values and early skills are first learned, before formal schooling begins. This first learning within the family is called primary socialisation.
notes.tip: Frame each point as the child's need being met, and say how it helps the child.

notes.b: Families do not meet every need alone. The State also helps with the cost and care of rearing children.
points: Education through schools, for example, gives every child the chance to learn and develop.
Child Benefit is a regular payment to parents for each child, which helps with the cost of rearing children.
Medical cards give access to medical care for families who qualify, so health needs are not left untreated because of cost.
Supports for disadvantaged pupils in school help children from poorer backgrounds to take part and do well.
Child-protection services through Tusla, the Child and Family Agency, protect children from harm.
notes.tip: State support is asked about as a way the State helps children or disadvantaged children. Give one example, such as Child Benefit, and say how it helps. Call it Child Benefit, not Children's Allowance.

notes.h: Rights of children within the family
notes.b: Children are not just dependants. They have rights, which are things every child is entitled to, and these are linked to the needs children have.
points: Right to life, and to a name and nationality, so the child has an identity and belongs to a country.
Right to be cared for by parents and to live with them, unless this would be contrary to the child's interests.
Right to protection from abuse and neglect, because children cannot defend themselves.
Right to education and to develop physically, mentally, socially, morally and spiritually.
Right to rest, play, leisure, culture and recreation, because play is how children learn and relax.
Right to protection from discrimination, so every child is treated fairly.
Right to maintenance, meaning financial support from parents. The duty of parents to maintain their children is in the Family Law (Maintenance of Spouses and Children) Act 1976.
Right to express an opinion and be heard in matters affecting the child, in line with age and maturity. Where parents live apart, children also have the right to see both parents.
notes.tip: When asked for four rights, give each right with a short account of what it means for the child, for example the right to education lets the child develop their abilities.

notes.h: Source of children's rights and the State's role
notes.b: Children's rights come from international and Irish law, and they are balanced with the duties of parents.
points: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child was adopted in 1989 and ratified by Ireland in 1992.
The Irish Constitution, since the Children Amendment, states the State's duty to protect children's rights.
Rights come with parents' duties, and the State steps in only where a child's welfare requires it.
The Child Care Act 1991 sets out the State's duty to protect children whose health, development or welfare is at risk.

The Child Care Act 1991 gives the State, through Tusla, the Child and Family Agency, powers to protect children at risk. These include care orders and emergency care orders, which can place the child outside the home, for example with foster carers.
notes.tip: Keep to these points on the Child Care Act: it gives Tusla powers to protect children at risk, including care orders and emergency care orders.

notes.h: Causes of conflict between adolescents and adults
notes.b: Conflict is common in adolescence because young people are moving towards adulthood while parents are still responsible for them. Most causes come back to the wish for independence.
points: Adolescents seek independence and may feel their parents are out of touch with them.
Peer and media influence can bring adolescents' values into conflict with the values of their parents.
Adolescents accept adult responsibilities but are not yet allowed adult freedoms, which causes frustration.
Relationships with peers and partners can take priority over schoolwork and family commitments, leading to disagreement.
Parents may struggle to let go gradually and trust young people, such as by allowing more freedom, while still needing to set limits.
Common flashpoints include curfews (a time to be home by), technology and money.
notes.tip: When explaining how relationships change in adolescence, link the change to independence, peer and media influence.

notes.h: Dealing with conflict between adolescents and adults
notes.b: Conflict is easier to resolve when both sides stay calm and work towards a solution together instead of trying to win.
points: Firm but fair discipline: rules are enforced consistently and, where possible, explained and agreed.
Listening and defining the issue: each side states its view and the problem is named clearly rather than made personal.
Negotiation and compromise: possible solutions are weighed together and reviewed after a trial period.
Home atmosphere: adolescents are more likely to resolve conflict when they feel free to talk to parents.
Parents can draw on their greater life experience while still hearing the young person's view.
Parents need to give trust gradually, so the young person has the chance to show responsibility.
notes.tip: A good answer on dealing with conflict covers firm but fair rules, communication and negotiation, with an explanation of each.

notes.b: Role-play lets you practise handling a disagreement, such as a curfew, in a safe way.
points: 1. Choose a conflict, for example an adolescent who wants a later curfew, and give one person the part of the adolescent and one the parent.
2. Each person states their view without interrupting, so each side feels heard.
3. Use "I" statements, such as "I feel left out when I have to leave early", so the other person is not blamed.
4. Name the problem clearly and suggest a compromise, for example a later curfew at weekends.
5. Agree a trial period and a time to review it, then discuss how it went.

notes.h: Importance of good communication in the family
notes.b: Communication is how family members share what they need and feel. Good communication keeps relationships strong and helps problems get solved.
points: Communication lets members express needs, feelings and opinions, so that each person feels heard, valued and secure.
Problems discussed openly are more likely to be solved before they become serious conflict.
Bottled-up feelings, such as anger kept hidden, can lead to resentment, stress and withdrawal.
Discussion of spending, meals, childcare and the care of vulnerable members allows household work to be shared fairly.
Explaining the reasons for rules, rather than simply imposing them, makes them more likely to be accepted.
Children learn language, empathy and negotiation by taking part in conversation with adults.
Older members who encourage and praise achievement build confidence in younger members.
Secrecy or aggressive criticism creates mistrust, loneliness and conflict.
notes.tip: When discussing the importance of communication, make each point and give its effect, for example problems are solved, shared decisions are made and confidence is built.

notes.b: Good communication is a skill, and it can be blocked by everyday habits.
points: Active listening means listening without interrupting, using calm language and checking understanding before replying.
Taking turns to speak gives everyone a chance to be heard, so no one person dominates.
Family meetings give a regular, planned time to discuss plans and problems, so issues are raised before they grow.
Barriers to communication include lack of time, screens, differences in age and tone of voice.

keyTerms.definition: The basic requirements for survival and growth, including food, shelter, clothing, warmth, sleep, health care and protection.
The emotional requirements for healthy development, including love, security, praise, stimulation and a sense of belonging.
The strong emotional bond formed between a young child and a consistent caregiver, which underpins security and trust.
A person's sense of their own worth, built through love, praise and experience of success.
Listening fully, without interrupting, and checking understanding before responding, so that the speaker feels heard.
A process in which two sides discuss differing views to reach an agreement both can accept.
An agreement in which each side gives up part of its position so that a solution can be reached.
A court order that places a child at risk under the care of the State, usually for a set period.
A short-term court order that removes a child from immediate danger when there is an urgent risk to the child's welfare.

factCards.term: Four physical needs of young children
factCards.definition: Food, shelter, clothing and protection from harm.

factCards.term: Four psychological needs of young children
factCards.definition: Love, security and trust, praise and encouragement, and learning stimulation.

factCards.term: Four rights of children within the family
factCards.definition: The right to life, name and nationality; the right to be raised by parents unless this is against the child's interests; the right to protection from abuse and neglect; and the right to education.

factCards.term: Three ways open communication prevents conflict
factCards.definition: Problems are raised before they escalate, rules are explained and agreed, and household plans are shared.

factCards.term: Three reasons adolescents and parents clash
factCards.definition: Adolescents seek independence; peer and media values differ from family values; and adults expect responsibility without granting matching freedom.

factCards.term: Four ways to deal with conflict between adolescents and adults
factCards.definition: Firm but fair discipline; listening and defining the issue; negotiation and compromise; and a home atmosphere where adolescents can talk freely.

questions.prompt: Outline three ways in which parents meet the psychological needs of young children.
questions.model: Any three, each with a brief explanation. Love and affection: warm physical and verbal affection shows the child is valued. Security and trust: a dependable, consistent caregiver makes the child feel safe. Praise and encouragement: recognising effort builds self-esteem. Stimulation: play, conversation and reading develop language and thinking. Routine and boundaries: consistent limits teach self-control.

questions.prompt: Discuss how the family meets the physical and psychological needs of adolescents, and explain how conflict between adolescents and adults can be managed.
questions.model: Needs: adolescents need food and sleep to support rapid growth, privacy and personal space, independence with gradually reduced parental control, a developing identity and self-esteem, peer acceptance, and emotional support when problems arise. Parents meet these needs through routines, respect for privacy, listening without judgement, and a gradual handover of responsibility. Conflict: caused by the search for independence, peer and media influence, the mismatch between adult responsibilities and adult freedoms, and competing priorities such as friendships over schoolwork. Management: firm but fair discipline with rules explained and agreed; listening and defining the issue clearly; negotiation and compromise with a review after a trial period; a home atmosphere where the adolescent feels free to talk. Full marks need the needs, how the family meets them, the causes of conflict and at least two management methods.
